content: Ancient DNA analysis has challenged a 150-year-old belief about a giant bird thought to have disappeared after the last Ice Age. For more than 150 years, scientists believed that enormous crane bones found in European caves belonged to a giant bird species that disappeared after the last Ice Age. Now, ancient DNA has overturned that identification, revealing that the supposedly extinct bird was actually a larger version of a species still living in Europe today. Researchers at Bournemouth University (BU) found that the fossils attributed to Grus primigenia belonged to the common crane. Their findings also raise questions about whether other prehistoric birds classified as extinct species were simply larger forms of birds that survive today. The mystery began in the 19th century when French biologist Alphonse Milne-Edwards examined unusually large crane bones discovered in caves in southern France. Believing they represented a distinct species, he named the bird Grus primigenia . The remains dated to the end of the last Ice Age and were long considered evidence of an extinct giant crane. To investigate the bird’s identity, a team led by Dr. John Stewart, Professor of Evolutionary Paleoecology at BU, analyzed ancient DNA from 18 crane bones recovered across England, Wales, France, Germany, and the Balearic Islands. Working with the Centre for Palaeogenetics in Stockholm, Sweden, the researchers used genetic evidence to determine which species the bones belonged to. “Previous studies had merely used the size and shape of the bones to attempt to understand these large birds. The use of DNA analysis has given us a more accurate picture of what they represent,” Stewart explained. The genetic findings indicate that the oversized fossils belonged to common cranes rather than a separate extinct species. Stewart believes differences in body size between male and female cranes may have contributed to the original misidentification. “We suspected that these large cranes were not extinct and instead represented larger, modern European common cranes. We believe that the reason for the mistaken identity was that cranes have large males and smaller females, and we think this contributed to previous speculation that there were two different species: the living, common crane we see today and the extinct, larger species,” Stewart said. Although the DNA evidence clarifies the birds’ identity, it leaves another question unanswered: Why were some prehistoric common cranes considerably larger than those living today? “The challenge going forward is to investigate the reason for the cranes decrease in size. Wetland drainage and human land use changes are what we suspect, but more work is needed to resolve that,” Stewart said. The researchers plan to investigate whether changes in wetland habitats and human land use contributed to the reduction in crane body size. These remain possible explanations rather than established causes. The findings suggest that some prehistoric bird species identified primarily through fossil measurements may need to be reconsidered. Differences in bone size do not necessarily indicate separate species, and ancient DNA could help determine whether other supposedly extinct birds were actually larger or smaller populations of surviving species. “While it is true that many species of birds are vulnerable to human actions today, it may be that we have overestimated the number of extinctions in the past,” Stewart said. “Some of these may instead represent size changes to living species,” he concluded. Reference: “Ancient DNA study resolves the taxonomic status of the extinct large Palaearctic crane Grus primigenia Milne-Edwards, 1871 (Aves: Gruiformes: Gruidae)” by John R. Stewart, Rebecca Rickard, Sheila Hamilton-Dyer, Keith Dobney, Veronique Laroulandie, Josep Antoni Alcover, Joan Femenias-Gual, Nadja Pöllath, Erik Ersmark, Bodil Cronholm, Per G. P. Ericson and Love Dalén, 1 October 2026, Royal Society Open Science . DOI: 10.1098/rsos.260699 Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter. Follow us on Google and Google News .

content: Astronomers have finally detected a mysterious, enormous dust structure in visible light, uncovering new details about what may be the remains of a violent collision between planetary bodies. Known as the “Cat’s Tail,” the feature stretches across as much as 1,000 astronomical units (about 93 billion miles) in the young Beta Pictoris star system. Located 63 light-years from Earth in the constellation Pictor (which is Latin for “painter”), Beta Pictoris is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rocky debris. The Cat’s Tail was discovered in infrared observations from the James Webb Space Telescope, but had remained hidden from telescopes observing shorter wavelengths. Now, new Hubble Space Telescope images, combined with observations spanning more than 14 years, are helping astronomers investigate its composition, geometry, and possible origins. “Oddly, this feature had previously only been seen with the James Webb Space Telescope, which detects infrared light, but remained invisible at shorter wavelengths, which has puzzled the community for a while,” said Arin Avsar, a doctoral student at the University of Arizona who led the research. The explanation may lie in the dust itself. “We think the Cat’s Tail has eluded our observations in visible light until now because of what it’s made of,” Avsar explained. “It consists almost entirely of we call organic refractory material, which is heavily carbon-based. These long chains of carbon atoms absorb visible light, so they’re quite black.” The observations also suggest that the structure contains microscopic dust grains with an exceptionally porous, fluffy composition. Although the particles are only about a micron across, their internal structure is difficult to explain through conventional models of planetary collisions. “How you can get dust grains that small that are as porous as we see here, no one really understands, and that’s part of why we study this feature,” Avsar said. Beta Pictoris is roughly 20 million years old, making it a valuable laboratory for studying the turbulent environments in which planets develop. Its debris disk contains material left behind from planet formation, including particles produced when larger objects collide. “The Cat’s Tail is thought to be the aftermath of a collision between large bodies – think something like Pluto,” said Avsar, who works with the research groups of Daniel Apai and Kevin Wagner at the University of Arizona’s Lunar and Planetary Laboratory and Steward Observatory. Such an impact could have scattered enormous quantities of dust, although the exact process that produced the observed particles remains uncertain. One possibility is that the impact generated enough heat to transform solid carbon into vapor, which later cooled and formed new particles. “It’s possible that the velocities involved in the collisions were so high that the carbon grains vaporized, turned into gas, and then recondensed as they cooled, and that’s how they became so porous,” said Wagner, a NASA Sagan Postdoctoral Fellow at Steward Observatory. The new observations have also changed astronomers’ understanding of the Cat’s Tail’s position in space. Earlier interpretations suggested that the feature extended far behind Beta Pictoris from Earth’s perspective, creating the appearance of a long structure stretching away from the star. By combining Hubble’s visible-light images with Webb’s infrared observations and computer modeling, the researchers developed a revised picture of its three-dimensional geometry. “We find that instead of extending for 1,000 astronomical units behind the star, the Cat’s Tail may extend straight sideways relative to us, and there is no third dimension to it,” Avsar said. “It’s essentially in the same plane of the sky as the star and possibly extends a little bit behind it.” The findings, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters , suggest that much of the structure’s apparent length lies across our field of view rather than extending deep into space. Its precise three-dimensional arrangement remains dependent on the models used to interpret the observations. Using Hubble in a new observing configuration, the team also identified a previously unseen warp in the dust halo surrounding Beta Pictoris. The distortion may result from the gravitational influence of Beta Pictoris b, one of three known planets in the system and a gas giant approximately 10 times Jupiter’s mass. “This gives us another line of evidence into how giant planets influence comets through their immense gravitational force,” Avsar said. “It’s a testament of how much these massive planets really influence their surrounding dust and icy bodies out to hundreds of astronomical units.” Similar gravitational interactions likely occurred during the early history of our solar system. When the Kuiper Belt was about 20 million years old, it may have contained hundreds of Pluto-sized objects packed into a much denser region than exists today. Over time, the gravitational influence of the giant planets altered the orbits of many of these bodies, scattering some into different regions or ejecting them from the solar system entirely. The Beta Pictoris observations provide a way to investigate comparable processes in a much younger planetary system, where collisions and gravitational disturbances are still shaping the distribution of material around its star. Reference: “Deep HST/STIS Coronagraphic Imaging of the β Pictoris Debris Disk: On the Scattered Light Component of the Cat’s Tail” by Arin M. Avsar, Kevin Wagner, Dániel Apai, Isabel Rebollido, Antranik A. Sefilian, Marshall D. Perrin, Christopher C. Stark, Gabriel Weible and András Gáspár, 7 October 2026, The Astrophysical Journal Letters . DOI: 10.3847/2041-8213/aeac4a Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter. title: South Korea targets 'world's highest performance' sovereign AI model in record new budget
content: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung unveiled the country's largest ever budget on Monday, pledging to "boldly invest in AI and future growth engines." Speaking to the National Assembly on Monday, Lee said total spending for 2027 would rise 12.8% to 820.9 trillion won ($610.14 billion), including 21.3 trillion won for semiconductors, physical AI and AI data centers — nearly double the 2026 level. A separate 4.7 trillion won will go toward developing a sovereign AI model with what Lee described as the "world's highest performance." The government also plans to invest heavily into talent, including training 2,000 specialists to "lead semiconductor design and the regional semiconductor industry," while expanding AI education for students, job seekers and existing workers. South Korea has set up university "contract departments," where students can enroll in company-linked degrees that offer pathways to jobs at firms like Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix before graduation. Companies help design courses, provide financial support and recruit qualifying graduates. The record spending plan comes as the International Monetary Fund forecasts South Korea's economy will grow 3.3% in 2026, its fastest pace since the post pandemic rebound in 2021. Lee said the higher spending would result in "virtually no net increase in government debt," with newly issued bonds used to repay existing debt. The budget also increases spending on defense and social security spending for the youth. Defense expenditure is set to rise 8.2% to 73.3 trillion won. "We will rapidly transform into a smart, elite, and powerful military by establishing a hybrid manned and unmanned system based on AI, robots, and drones," Lee said. South Korea's strong economic growth has been driven largely by semiconductor exports as global demand for computing power rises with the AI boom. Exports surged 93.7% from a year earlier to a record $115.3 billion in October, according to data released Sunday by the Korea Customs Service. Shipments totaled $930 billion in the first 10 months of 2026, surpassing the $900 billion mark for the first time. The country posted a $42.5 billion trade surplus in October, with imports rising 36% year on year to $72.8 billion. Lee said South Korea was within reach of $1 trillion in annual exports, citing strong performance in key industries including semiconductors.
